text.hook:
Condition variables look simple. Then the interviewer asks what happens to the mutex inside wait().

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. 📌
text.body:
Inside:
1. The three pieces and their jobs
2. What wait() does, step by step
3. Why the predicate loop is mandatory
4. notify_one vs notify_all, and clean shutdown
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Save it for your next interview.

first_comment: 🧠 Test yourself: can two threads wait on the same `std::condition_variable` while using different mutexes? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No. All threads concurrently waiting on one std::condition_variable must use the same mutex, otherwise it is undefined behaviour.

slides.lead: A condition variable is a doorbell, not a mailbox. Here is what that means in an interview.

slides.title: Three pieces, three jobs
rows: The actual condition. The **only** thing that is remembered.
Protects the state and orders its reads and writes (happens-before).
Lets a thread block efficiently and be woken when the state *may* have changed.
slides.takeaway: Wait for the state, not for the notification.

slides.title: What happens to the mutex
steps: **Atomically** release the mutex and register as a waiter. No gap between the two.
Block until `notify_one`, `notify_all`, a spurious wakeup, or a timeout.
Reacquire the mutex. This is a normal lock and may block again.
Return. The mutex is **always** held when `wait` returns.

slides.title: `wait(lock, pred)` is specified as a loop
bullets: **Spurious wakeup:** `wait` may return with no notify at all.
**Stolen wakeup:** another consumer got the mutex first and took the item.
**Shared CV:** the notify was about a different condition.
slides.takeaway: Checked **before** blocking: if `pred()` is already true, the thread never sleeps.

slides.title: notify_one or notify_all?
rows: Waiters on one CV wait for different predicates
Waiter may destroy the CV right after waking
slides.takeaway: The state change must be under the mutex. Where you notify is mostly a performance choice.

slides.title: The worker pool pattern
items: Put `stopping` in the predicate, or workers can never wake for it
`notify_all`, not `notify_one`: every worker must see it
Drain or abandon queued work, on purpose

slides.lead: A notify with no waiter is simply dropped. A semaphore `release()` before `acquire()` is not lost. With a CV, your predicate is the memory.

items.truth: The CV knows nothing about your state. Your predicate checks it, under the mutex.

items.myth: "If I hold the mutex, how can another thread change `ready`?"
items.truth: You do not hold it while blocked in `wait`. That is the whole point.

items.myth: "The CV remembers a notify that happened before I waited."
items.truth: It is dropped. Only the predicate remembers.

items.myth: "Wake-up plus mutex reacquisition is one atomic step."
items.truth: Only release-and-register is atomic. Reacquiring is a normal lock that can block.

items.myth: "A spurious wakeup is a notification sent by mistake."
items.truth: It is a return from `wait` with no matching notification. The standard allows it.
It only means the time did not run out. Always re-check the state.

slides.hero:
Mutex: protects the state.
Predicate: is the state.
CV: only the doorbell.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
The producer sets ready = true and notifies.
Only then does the consumer start waiting.

What is printed? Comment your answer, then swipe ➜ to check it.
text.body: Four plausible outputs. One rule about notifications decides which one you will see.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: `while (!ready) cv.wait_for(lk, 1s);` is meant to wait at most 1 second. Why can it wait forever? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Every wakeup restarts the 1 s timeout, so unrelated notifications every 200 ms postpone it forever. Use `cv.wait_for(lk, 1s, pred)`: one fixed deadline.

slides.title: Producer finishes first. Output?

slides.verdict_sub: after blocking for the full 200 ms
bullets: `notify_one` ran when nobody was waiting, so it was **dropped**. CVs do not remember notifications.
The raw `wait_for` blocks the full 200 ms, although `ready` was `true` the whole time.
With a plain `cv.wait(lk)` it would hang forever.
A spurious wakeup could in theory print `no_timeout`. That would not mean anything was signalled either.

slides.title: Wait for the state, not the notification
slides.takeaway: The predicate is checked first. A notify that came "too early" is harmless with the predicate form.

text.body: There are two problems here, and the first one is worse.

first_comment: 🧠 Follow-up: readers want to wait on a condition while holding a `std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex>`. Can std::condition_variable do that? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No. It only accepts std::unique_lock<std::mutex>. Use std::condition_variable_any, which works with other lock types (and a stop_token in C++20), at some size and speed cost.

slides.title:
The producer skips the mutex.
What is true?

slides.verdict: D. A data race, then a lost wakeup
slides.verdict_sub: ThreadSanitizer flags `ready = true` on the first run
bullets: The write races with the predicate's read of `ready`: undefined behaviour.
Protection needs **both** sides to lock. Here only one does.
The CV orders nothing. The mutex does: unlock *synchronizes-with* the next lock.
It also reopens the lost-wakeup window.

slides.title: Change the state under the mutex, then notify
slides.tip: Run CV code under `-fsanitize=thread`: it reports this race immediately.
slides.takeaway: The mutex protects the predicate. `notify` only rings the bell.

text.body: Two numbers to predict: how often the predicate runs, and whether the lock is held at the end.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: why does `cv.wait` refuse a `std::lock_guard` and insist on `std::unique_lock`? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: `wait` must unlock the mutex while blocked and relock it before returning. `lock_guard` has no `unlock()`/`lock()`, so passing it does not compile.

slides.title:
Nobody ever calls notify.
What is printed?

bullets: `wait(lk, pred)` is `while (!pred()) wait(lk);`.
The predicate runs once, **before** any blocking. It is already `true`.
So the thread never sleeps and no notification is needed.
The lock was never released, so it is still owned on return.

slides.title: The predicate form is a loop
bullets: Checked **before** blocking: a notify sent before the wait is harmless.
Re-checked after **every** wakeup, always with the mutex held.
slides.takeaway: A CV wait on an already-true condition costs one function call.

text.hook:
notify_one(): inside the lock, or after unlocking?
Code reviewers argue about this all the time.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The right answer separates correctness from performance, then adds one important exception.

first_comment: 🧠 Follow-up: five threads wait on one CV. Does notify_one wake the one that has waited longest? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Not guaranteed. Which waiter wakes is unspecified, so a CV-based queue is not FIFO-fair. If fairness matters, use a ticketed design or one CV per thread.

slides.title:
The waiter checks `done`.
Which producer is correct?
options: Only 1: it hands over the mutex

slides.verdict_sub: The state change must be under the mutex. The notify need not be.
bullets: 1: the waiter may wake, find the mutex still held, and block again ("hurry up and wait").
2: fewer wasted context switches.
No lost wakeup in 2: `done` was changed under the mutex.
A notify never hands over the mutex. The woken thread competes for it.
slides.wrong: "Notify after unlock can lose the wakeup"

slides.title: When version 2 is a bug
slides.tip: TSan: heap-use-after-free in `notify_one`. Under the lock, the waiter cannot return first.
slides.takeaway: State under the mutex for correctness. Notify after unlock for speed, unless the waiter may destroy the CV.

text.hook:
notify_all() wakes three consumers.
C1 grabs the mutex and holds it for 40 seconds.
Do C2 and C3 need another notify?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Two kinds of waiting hide in this question. Interviewers check whether you can tell them apart.

first_comment: 🧠 Follow-up: the whole condition is one atomic flag. Which C++20 tool lets a thread sleep on it with no mutex and no CV? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: `flag.wait(old)` on the std::atomic: it blocks while the value equals old. The setter stores the new value first, then calls `flag.notify_one()` (or notify_all).

slides.title:
3 items, one `notify_all()`, C1 wins.
What do C2 and C3 do?
options: Block on the mutex, no new notify
Sleep on the CV until a new notify
Spin on the mutex, burning CPU

slides.verdict_sub: Run with 1 s instead of 40 s: items taken at 0.1 s, 1.1 s, 2.1 s, one notify
bullets: `notify_all` already woke them. They left the CV and now wait **for the mutex**.
Waiting on the CV needs a notify. Waiting for the mutex ends when it is free.
`wait` returns only with the mutex held, so `process` runs one at a time.
Whether a mutex spins briefly is up to the implementation. Mainstream ones block in the kernel.

slides.title: Pop, unlock, then process
slides.tip: Holding the mutex for 40 s blocks every consumer and every producer.
slides.takeaway: Notification and mutex acquisition are separate events. Keep the locked region tiny.
